variants.title: Separate meaning from mechanics
variants.context: An HTTP version changes delivery mechanics, not business meaning. Semantics (methods, status codes, caching, authorization) stay; expression (framing and compression) and transport (TCP vs QUIC) change.
variants.prompt: A POST is sent over HTTP/3. Is it safe to retry because QUIC is reliable?
options: No. Retry safety is an application contract, not a transport one.
Yes, QUIC guarantees exactly-once delivery of the request.
Yes, provided the client retries the POST only once.
optionFeedback: A POST is not idempotent because it crossed QUIC.
Reliable transport is not exactly-once application effect.
One retry is still a second request, and the server may have committed the first.
variants.hint: Which layer decides whether a request is idempotent?
variants.explanation: HTTP versions change framing and transport, never business meaning.

variants.title: Separate meaning from mechanics
variants.context: An HTTP version changes delivery mechanics, not business meaning. Semantics (methods, status codes, caching, authorization) stay; expression (framing and compression) and transport (TCP vs QUIC) change.
variants.prompt: Which parts change between HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3?
options: Framing, field compression, and transport, not the semantics.
Everything changes, including methods and status codes.
Only the default port number and the TLS handshake.
optionFeedback: HTTP/1.1 is textual, HTTP/2 binary frames with HPACK over TCP, HTTP/3 QUIC streams with QPACK.
Semantics are shared across versions; a 404 means the same thing on all three.
The change reaches framing, compression, and transport, far deeper than a port.
variants.hint: What does a cache or an authorization check need to know about the version?
variants.explanation: The expression and transport layers change; the semantic contract is the same.

variants.title: Separate meaning from mechanics
variants.context: An HTTP version changes delivery mechanics, not business meaning. Semantics (methods, status codes, caching, authorization) stay; expression (framing and compression) and transport (TCP vs QUIC) change.
variants.prompt: A browser negotiates HTTP/3 to the edge. Does that describe the whole request path?
options: Yes, the negotiated version applies for the whole path.
Only when the origin also advertises HTTP/3 support.
No. The edge may use HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 upstream.
optionFeedback: Each hop negotiates separately, so the browser describes only its own leg.
Origin support does not change what the edge chose upstream.
Versions can coexist per hop for one origin, so record the protocol on every hop.
variants.hint: How many connections does a request cross?
variants.explanation: Record the protocol per hop instead of assuming the browser’s version describes the path.

variants.title: Follow one HTTP/2 request
variants.context: An HTTP/2 request belongs to one stream: open the stream, send the field section (HEADERS), interleave content (DATA) with other streams, and close each direction independently (END_STREAM).
variants.prompt: A browser fetches an image over an existing HTTP/2 connection. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Close each direction independently with END_STREAM.
Send the HEADERS field section with :method, :scheme, :authority, and :path.
Open a stream with a new stream identifier.
Exchange DATA frames, interleaved with frames from other streams.

variants.hint: A stream has an explicit lifecycle from idle to closed.
variants.explanation: Open → HEADERS → DATA → END_STREAM. A stream error resets one exchange; a connection error affects every stream.

variants.title: Follow one HTTP/2 request
variants.context: An HTTP/2 request belongs to one stream: open the stream, send the field section (HEADERS), interleave content (DATA) with other streams, and close each direction independently (END_STREAM).
variants.prompt: A slow API response and a fast image share one connection. Put the steps for the image in order.

items.text: It sends the field section, HPACK-indexing repeated fields.
The image’s DATA frames interleave with the slow response’s frames.
The client opens a new stream for the image.
The image stream closes while the slow stream stays open.

variants.hint: Interleaving is why one slow response does not monopolize the connection.
variants.explanation: Frames from many streams interleave; each stream closes on its own.

variants.title: Follow one HTTP/2 request
variants.context: An HTTP/2 request belongs to one stream: open the stream, send the field section (HEADERS), interleave content (DATA) with other streams, and close each direction independently (END_STREAM).
variants.prompt: A server cancels one response without dropping the connection. Put the steps in order.

items.text: The server resets that stream only; other streams continue.
DATA was flowing among other streams.
The stream was opened with its own identifier.

variants.hint: Stream errors and connection errors have different scopes.
variants.explanation: A stream error can reset one exchange while the connection keeps serving the rest.

variants.title: Reason about loss
variants.context: HTTP/2 streams are independent, but TCP delivers one ordered byte stream, so a lost segment blocks unrelated streams until repaired. QUIC recovers loss per stream; connection-wide congestion control still applies. QPACK can still block on a missing dynamic-table insert.
variants.prompt: One TCP segment carrying frames for stream 5 is lost. Can frames for stream 7 that arrived after it be delivered to the HTTP/2 parser?
options: Yes, because the streams are logically independent.
Yes, provided stream 7 carries a higher priority.
No. TCP presents one ordered byte stream to the parser.
optionFeedback: Independence is logical; delivery is one ordered stream.
Priority is a scheduling hint, not a transport property.
Logical independence does not remove TCP ordering, so later bytes wait for the repair.
variants.hint: What does the parser receive from TCP?
variants.explanation: HTTP/2 over TCP suffers transport head-of-line blocking across streams.

variants.title: Reason about loss
variants.context: HTTP/2 streams are independent, but TCP delivers one ordered byte stream, so a lost segment blocks unrelated streams until repaired. QUIC recovers loss per stream; connection-wide congestion control still applies. QPACK can still block on a missing dynamic-table insert.
variants.prompt: The same loss happens on an HTTP/3 connection. What is different?
options: HTTP/3 never loses packets, because QUIC retransmits.
Only the affected QUIC stream waits; the others deliver.
Nothing, because one loss still blocks every stream.
optionFeedback: Loss still happens on QUIC; what changes is that recovery is stream-aware.
QUIC recovers loss per stream.
Per-stream recovery is exactly the HTTP/3 change, so unrelated streams keep going.
variants.hint: At which layer does QUIC recover loss?
variants.explanation: Connection-wide congestion control and flow control still apply; per-stream recovery is what improves.

variants.title: Reason about loss
variants.context: HTTP/2 streams are independent, but TCP delivers one ordered byte stream, so a lost segment blocks unrelated streams until repaired. QUIC recovers loss per stream; connection-wide congestion control still applies. QPACK can still block on a missing dynamic-table insert.
variants.prompt: Does QPACK guarantee that field decoding never blocks?
options: It blocks only when the connection runs over TCP.
No. A dynamic reference can block until its insert arrives.
Yes, preventing that block is exactly its purpose.
optionFeedback: QPACK is an HTTP/3 mechanism and never runs over TCP at all.
QPACK reduces the problem HPACK would create over independent streams; it does not eliminate blocking.
Static references never block, but dynamic ones can, so bound the blocked streams.
variants.hint: Which references depend on state that may not have arrived yet?
variants.explanation: Bound dynamic-table capacity and SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS; treat control-stream loss as a connection-level signal.

variants.title: Retire the old assumption
variants.context: RFC 9113 deprecated the original priority tree; RFC 9218 defines urgency 0–7 (smaller is higher) and an incremental flag. Server push is optional legacy: Chromium disabled it by default from Chrome 106.
variants.prompt: A team designs around the HTTP/2 dependency-and-weight priority tree. What should they know?
options: The priority tree is honored end to end by servers.
RFC 9113 deprecated it; RFC 9218 defines urgency instead.
It is still the standard scheme for HTTP/2 today.
optionFeedback: Priority is a hint, and an endpoint may schedule differently or ignore it entirely.
Use the Priority field and PRIORITY_UPDATE frames; test that the stack applies them.
The original dependency and weight scheme is deprecated, so do not build on it.
variants.hint: Which RFC describes current priority signals?
variants.explanation: Priority is a scheduling hint. Monitor critical-resource completion instead of trusting the signal.

variants.title: Retire the old assumption
variants.context: RFC 9113 deprecated the original priority tree; RFC 9218 defines urgency 0–7 (smaller is higher) and an incremental flag. Server push is optional legacy: Chromium disabled it by default from Chrome 106.
variants.prompt: A page relies on HTTP/2 server push for its critical CSS. Why is that risky?
options: Push is optional legacy, and clients can disable it.
Push always beats a cache hit for critical CSS.
Push is required by HTTP/3 and always available.
optionFeedback: Chromium turned push off by default from Chrome 106; optimize cacheability instead.
A cache hit costs no bytes at all, and pushed bytes are often already cached.
HTTP/3 does not require push either, and major clients ignore it.
variants.explanation: Never require server push for correctness or acceptable latency.

variants.title: Retire the old assumption
variants.context: RFC 9113 deprecated the original priority tree; RFC 9218 defines urgency 0–7 (smaller is higher) and an incremental flag. Server push is optional legacy: Chromium disabled it by default from Chrome 106.
variants.prompt: Which urgency value has the highest precedence under RFC 9218?
options: 7, the largest value.
Whatever the server chooses.
0, the smallest value.
optionFeedback: 7 is the lowest urgency.
Endpoints may ignore signals, but the scale is defined.
Smaller numbers mean higher precedence.
variants.hint: Which direction does the scale run?
variants.explanation: Urgency runs from 0 (highest) to 7 (lowest); incremental marks responses useful as chunks arrive.

variants.title: Count the streams
variants.context: SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS caps open peer-initiated streams; new work waits or uses another connection. Flow control credits DATA at stream and connection level and is not a request scheduler.
variants.prompt: An HTTP/1.1 client opens six connections to run six responses concurrently. On HTTP/2 with SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS at 100, how many connections do those six concurrent responses need?
variants.explanation: One connection carries all six as separate streams, saving separate congestion-control and connection costs.

mistakes.feedback: That is the HTTP/1.1 model; HTTP/2 multiplexes.
That is the stream cap, not a connection count.

variants.title: Count the streams
variants.context: SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS caps open peer-initiated streams; new work waits or uses another connection. Flow control credits DATA at stream and connection level and is not a request scheduler.
variants.prompt: A peer advertises SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS of 100 and a client has 250 requests ready. How many must wait or use another connection?
variants.hint: Subtract the cap from the ready requests.
variants.explanation: 250 − 100 = 150 requests wait for streams to close or go to another connection.

mistakes.feedback: That is how many can run, not how many wait.

variants.title: Count the streams
variants.context: SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS caps open peer-initiated streams; new work waits or uses another connection. Flow control credits DATA at stream and connection level and is not a request scheduler.
variants.prompt: RFC 9218 urgency values run from 0 through 7. How many urgency levels exist?
variants.explanation: 0 through 7 is eight levels, with 0 the highest precedence.

mistakes.feedback: The range is inclusive on both ends.
